I just pulled in 17 MILLION VIEWS last month for my startup, all on one account… Here’s how I engineer virality: - Study what’s working in my niche and recreate the top videos - A/B/C/D/E testing on hooks, pacing, captions, story - Use Vyra to autonomously edit 20 versions of the same video to test - Force my cofounder Caleb to make an appearance (our most viral video had both of us in it :D) When we landed in SF six weeks ago, we had 0 views, 0 followers, 0 traction. The growth has been genuinely insane…and there’s so much more to come :) Try Vyra for yourself and let us know what you think! And lmk if you’re in SF…let’s touch grass and talk content together!

Imagine humanoids that can work around people safely and autonomously. At UW CSE / RAIVN Lab, we built a fully autonomous vision-based human localization and following policy for humanoid robots. The policy can search for a person by actively rotating, recover when the person is behind the robot, and maintain a safe distance while following. I’m excited about this direction because it connects vision, embodied AI, and real-world robot deployment: perception is not just recognizing what is in front of the camera, but deciding where to look, how to move, and how to stay safe around humans. Huge shout-out to the team. #Robotics #EmbodiedAI #ComputerVision #HumanoidRobots

𝙄’𝙢 𝙧𝙚𝙖𝙡𝙡𝙮 𝙜𝙡𝙖𝙙 𝙬𝙚 𝙛𝙤𝙡𝙡𝙤𝙬𝙚𝙙 𝙩𝙝𝙧𝙤𝙪𝙜𝙝 𝙬𝙞𝙩𝙝 𝙞𝙩.” Soon after, DubOps was named the 𝗔𝗪𝗦 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗿, with each member receiving an HP EliteBook 14” laptop. Purple is here! 💜-> https://lnkd.in/gAwrJxSe After months of building and evaluating, the University of Washington 's own generative AI platform is officially live for faculty and staff! I started at University of Washington Information Technology on the networking team under Shane Ryan McDowell before moving to the AI team, where I got the incredible opportunity to help build Purple from the ground up. As an AI Intern at UWIT, here's some of what I built to help get us to launch: - Built a 𝗣𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝘆𝘄𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗔/𝗕 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹-𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺: blind comparisons (e.g., GPT-4o vs. newer variants) scored by an 𝗟𝗟𝗠-𝗮𝘀-𝗷𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗲 rubric across five dimensions, exported to reports that drove model-selection decisions for platform leadership. - Developed 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗔𝗜 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 across a wide range of use cases, engineering each with purpose-built starter prompts, usage-driven guardrails, and scoped boundaries grounded in how real users interact with the system. - Engineered and benchmarked prompts for system-level agents serving 𝟲𝟬𝗸+ 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘀, iterating against eval metrics through systematic prompt engineering. - Orchestrated 𝗹𝗼𝗮𝗱 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝗱-𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 across all agents via 𝗖𝗜 𝗽𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 to harden them ahead of launch. I've learned that at scale, the hard part of AI engineering isn't the model, it's everything around it. 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘀, 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆, and the weight of knowing a single prompt change reaches 60,000 people. Huge congrats to the entire UWIT team and special thanks to my mentors Jared Reimer and Christa Hickcox, Technology Leader, AI, Coach, DEI for the trust and autonomy to take initiative, learn by doing, and deliver real things on my own. It has also been amazing working with people like William Casas and Collin Globig on the Cloudforce team! And none of this could have happened without Shane Ryan McDowell and the rest of 𝗨𝗪𝗜𝗧, who gave me my start and the foundation to grow into this role. On a personal note: I am 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗙𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽𝘀 in AI engineering and SWE. If your team is building in this space, I'd love to connect! #AI #GenerativeAI #SoftwareEngineering #AIEngineering #UW #TechInternship

I set up this LinkedIn account years ago, but I didn't bother posting as I always assumed my network would come through the military. I started college as an Air Force ROTC cadet, and I built my identity around that path. I thrived in the structure, the discipline, the commitment to the future I thought I was stepping into. Then I was medically disqualified in late February. I accepted the news with hopes of overturning the decision, but I couldn't get it waived. My grades and my energy dipped these past two quarters, and it was humbling to realize how much of my confidence and performance came from that external structure and discipline. However, losing my original path didn’t make me smaller: it made me more well‑rounded. That identity loss was the catalyst for me to explore activities such as martial arts or bible study, and I found myself able to commit to responsibilities such as undergraduate research or club leadership. These past 4 months have taught me that people don't thrive because they're "disciplined", they thrive because of the support of those around them. If I had to sum up this chapter in a single word, it would be community. I’m deeply grateful to the people who helped me rebuild this past quarter – my family, and the cadre and cadets at Detachment 910. I also want to recognize my roommate, Matthew Kroes , for his constant support through every high and low, and Hannah Tan for welcoming me into a wonderful Christian group. I’m equally grateful to the Husky Flying Club leadership who welcomed me into my next chapter and believed in what I could contribute: • Former President – Hugh Suratgar • Former VP – Orest Brykowytch • Current President – Jack Eckhart With their support, I’m excited to share that I’ll be stepping into the role of Vice President of the Husky Flying Club. For me, the Husky Flying Club isn't just an organization that puts aircraft, pilots, and engineers in the same room. It's a community to train undergraduates to become career ready. In many ways, it's similar to ROTC. As VP, my focus this incoming school year is to prepare HFC for that mission by applying the lessons from ROTC to our club. From strengthening communication to providing opportunities for incoming members, I look forward to working with our wonderful team to build a culture structured to cultivate students. Although there is much to be done, I'm most excited about serving the community that guided me throughout my first half of university. It’s a chance to give back, support the incoming classes of aviators and engineers, and grow into the kind of leader who lifts others the way others lifted me. Cheers to the next chapter. – Albert Hengyucius
